title: How bees find flowers
subject: Biology
text: Honeybees rely on several senses to find food. From a distance, they are drawn by color, and many flowers reflect ultraviolet light that bees can see but people cannot. Up close, scent becomes more important, guiding the bee to the exact part of the flower that holds nectar. Bees also share what they find. A worker returning to the hive performs a dance whose direction and length tell other bees where the flowers are and how far away they lie. In this way, a colony can quickly focus its effort on the richest sources of food.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what helps bees find flowers from far away?
choices: Color, including ultraviolet light
Scent from the nectar
Sounds made by other bees
The temperature of the flower
questions.explanation: *From a distance, they are drawn by color*, including ultraviolet light.

questions.stem: The word "richest" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: most productive
most expensive
most beautiful
most distant
questions.explanation: Rich sources of food are the ones that give the most food: most productive.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the dance?
choices: To explain how bees share the location of food
To show that bees enjoy music
To describe how bees build the hive
To compare bees with other insects
questions.explanation: The dance tells other bees where the flowers are.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a flower that reflects no ultraviolet light?
choices: It may be harder for bees to notice from far away
Bees cannot collect its nectar
It has no scent
Bees will never visit it
questions.explanation: Bees are drawn from a distance partly by ultraviolet light, so such a flower would be less visible to them from afar. The other choices go beyond the passage.

title: The first cities
subject: History
text: The earliest cities appeared in Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago. They grew up near rivers, where farmers could water their fields and produce more food than their families needed. This surplus allowed some people to stop farming and become potters, builders, priests or record keepers. To track the grain stored in temples, officials developed a system of marks pressed into clay tablets. Over time, these marks became one of the world's first writing systems. Cities, in other words, did not only bring people together; they also created the need for new ways to organize information.

questions.stem: Why could some people in early cities stop farming?
choices: Farmers produced more food than they needed
The government paid them to stop
The rivers flooded the fields
They moved to other cities
questions.explanation: The surplus of food let some people take other jobs.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about early writing?
choices: It began partly as a way to keep records
It was invented by potters
It was used mainly for poetry
It appeared before the first cities
questions.explanation: Marks used to track stored grain developed into writing, so writing began with record keeping.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Early cities created new jobs and new ways of handling information
Mesopotamia had the best farmland in the world
Clay tablets were difficult to make
Priests were the most powerful people in early cities
questions.explanation: The final sentence sums up: cities brought people together and created new ways to organize information.

title: Why the sky is blue
subject: Physics
text: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. When it passes through the atmosphere, it meets tiny molecules of gas. These molecules scatter short wavelengths of light, such as blue, much more strongly than long wavelengths, such as red. As a result, blue light is sent in every direction across the sky, and that is the color we see when we look up. At sunrise and sunset, light must travel through much more air to reach us. By then most of the blue has been scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges that color the evening sky.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which kind of light is scattered most strongly by gas molecules?
choices: Light with short wavelengths, such as blue
Light with long wavelengths, such as red
White light
Light from the moon
questions.explanation: Molecules scatter short wavelengths, such as blue, more strongly.

questions.stem: Why is the sky red at sunset?
choices: Light passes through more air, so most blue light is scattered away
The sun becomes cooler in the evening
Clouds reflect red light
Gas molecules change color at night
questions.explanation: At sunset light travels through more air, and most of the blue is scattered away.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, why would the sky look less blue if the atmosphere were much thinner?
choices: There would be fewer molecules to scatter blue light
Sunlight would contain no blue light
Red light would be scattered more strongly
The sun would be farther away
questions.explanation: Blue sky comes from molecules scattering short wavelengths. Fewer molecules means less scattering.

title: Sleep and memory
subject: Psychology
text: Scientists once thought the brain simply rested during sleep. Research now shows that sleep plays an active role in memory. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity from the day, strengthening the connections that store new information. In experiments, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than students who stayed awake for the same length of time. Lack of sleep, by contrast, makes it harder both to learn new material and to recall what was learned before. For students preparing for an exam, a full night of sleep may be worth more than a few extra hours of study.

questions.stem: What did the experiment described in the passage show?
choices: Students who slept after learning remembered more
Students who stayed awake learned faster
Sleep has no effect on memory
Students remember lists better than stories
questions.explanation: Students who slept remembered more of the words the next day.

questions.stem: The word "recall" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: remember
repeat
forget
review
questions.explanation: To recall what was learned is to remember it.

questions.stem: What would the author most likely advise a student the night before an exam?
choices: Get a full night of sleep
Study all night
Learn a new list of words
Take a long nap in the afternoon
questions.explanation: The last sentence says a full night of sleep may be worth more than extra study.

title: Coral reefs
subject: Ecology
text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all marine species. A reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which take calcium from seawater to form hard skeletons. Inside the polyps live algae that use sunlight to make food, and they share this food with the coral. This partnership is easily disturbed. When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae and turns white, a process called bleaching. If the water cools quickly, the coral may recover, but long periods of heat can kill large parts of a reef.

questions.stem: What do the algae provide to the coral?
choices: Food made with sunlight
Calcium for skeletons
Protection from fish
Cooler water
questions.explanation: The algae use sunlight to make food, and they share it with the coral.

questions.stem: What causes coral bleaching?
choices: Water that becomes too warm
Too much sunlight
Too many fish on the reef
Water that is too cold
questions.explanation: When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae and turns white.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor?
choices: To stress how many species depend on a small area
To show that reefs are disappearing
To explain how reefs are built
To compare reefs with forests
questions.explanation: *Yet* contrasts the tiny area with the quarter of all marine species that live there.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about a reef after a short period of very warm water?
choices: It may recover if the water cools quickly
It will certainly die
It will grow faster than before
It will lose all its fish permanently
questions.explanation: The passage says the coral may recover if the water cools quickly; only long periods of heat kill large parts of a reef.

title: The invention of paper money
subject: Economics
text: For most of history, people paid for goods with metal coins, which were heavy to carry in large amounts. In China, around the eleventh century, merchants began leaving their coins with trusted shops and receiving paper receipts in return. These receipts could be traded, and soon they were accepted as payment in their own right. The government later took control of printing them, creating some of the first official paper money. Paper money worked only as long as people trusted that it could be exchanged for something of value. When governments printed too much of it, prices rose and the money lost that trust.

questions.stem: How did paper money begin in China, according to the passage?
choices: As receipts for coins left with trusted shops
As a gift from the government
As decorations for festivals
As tickets for travel
questions.explanation: Merchants left coins with shops and received paper receipts, which began to be traded.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about printing too much money?
choices: It can make money less valuable
It makes coins heavier
It increases trust in the government
It has no effect on prices
questions.explanation: Printing too much made prices rise and the money lose trust, so it lost value.

title: How volcanoes form islands
subject: Geology
text: Some islands form far from the edges of the earth's plates, in the middle of the ocean. Geologists explain them with the idea of hot spots. A hot spot is a place where unusually hot rock rises from deep within the earth and melts near the surface, producing volcanoes on the sea floor. Over time, a volcano can grow tall enough to rise above the water. Because the plate above the hot spot moves slowly, the volcano is gradually carried away from its source and becomes inactive, while a new volcano forms over the hot spot. The result is a chain of islands that grow older the farther they are from the hot spot.

questions.stem: What is a hot spot?
choices: A place where hot rock rises and melts near the surface
A warm part of the ocean
An island with many volcanoes
The edge of a plate
questions.explanation: The passage defines it as a place where unusually hot rock rises and melts near the surface.

questions.stem: In a chain of islands formed by a hot spot, which island is likely to be the oldest?
choices: The island farthest from the hot spot
The island directly over the hot spot
The largest island
The island with the most active volcano
questions.explanation: The islands grow older the farther they are from the hot spot.

title: Early photography
subject: Art history
text: The first photographs, made in the 1820s and 1830s, required exposures lasting minutes or even hours. As a result, early photographers chose subjects that did not move, such as buildings and landscapes. Portraits were possible but uncomfortable: sitters had to hold perfectly still, sometimes with their heads held in place by hidden metal stands. This explains why people in many early portraits look stiff and serious. As chemical processes improved, exposure times fell to seconds, and photographers could capture more natural expressions and, eventually, moving scenes.

questions.stem: Why did early photographers often photograph buildings?
choices: Buildings did not move during long exposures
Buildings were cheaper to photograph
People did not want to be photographed
Buildings looked better in black and white
questions.explanation: Exposures lasted minutes or hours, so they chose subjects that did not move.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention hidden metal stands?
choices: To show how difficult it was to sit for an early portrait
To describe the cameras of the time
To explain how buildings were photographed
To show that photographers were careless
questions.explanation: Stands held heads still, showing how uncomfortable early portraits were.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about photographs of busy streets taken in the 1830s?
choices: Moving people would barely appear in them
They showed crowds clearly
They were taken at night
They were in color
questions.explanation: Exposures lasted minutes, so anything moving would blur or vanish; that is why early photographers chose still subjects.

title: Language and the brain
subject: Linguistics
text: Children learn their first language without formal lessons, yet by the age of five most can use complex grammar. Some researchers argue that humans are born with a special ability for language, which explains how quickly children learn. Others stress the role of experience, noting that children hear millions of words in their first years and are highly sensitive to patterns in that speech. Today many scientists combine these views. They suggest that children are born with powerful general learning abilities and a strong interest in communication, and that these abilities, applied to the language around them, are enough to explain their success.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do researchers who stress experience point out?
choices: Children hear millions of words in their early years
Children are taught grammar in school
Adults learn languages faster than children
Language ability is inherited from parents
questions.explanation: They note that children hear millions of words and are sensitive to patterns.

questions.stem: How is the passage organized?
choices: It presents two views and then a view that combines them
It describes a single experiment in detail
It lists the stages of language learning in order
It argues against all theories of language
questions.explanation: It gives the inborn view, the experience view, and then a combined view.

title: Desert plants
subject: Botany
text: Plants in deserts face two problems: little rain and strong sun. Many have developed ways to save water. Cacti store water in thick stems and have spines instead of broad leaves, which reduces the surface from which water can evaporate. Some desert plants open their pores only at night, when the air is cooler and less water is lost. Others avoid the dry season entirely. Their seeds lie in the soil for years and sprout only after heavy rain, so the plants grow, flower and produce new seeds in just a few weeks.

questions.stem: Why do cacti have spines instead of broad leaves?
choices: To reduce the surface that loses water
To attract insects
To store water
To make food at night
questions.explanation: Spines reduce the surface from which water can evaporate.

questions.stem: How do some plants avoid the dry season?
choices: Their seeds wait in the soil until heavy rain
They move to wetter places
They grow very deep roots
They lose all their leaves
questions.explanation: Their seeds lie in the soil for years and sprout only after heavy rain.

questions.stem: Why do some desert plants probably open their pores only at night?
choices: They lose less water in the cooler night air
They need moonlight to make food
Insects visit them only at night
The soil is wetter in the evening
questions.explanation: The passage says night air is cooler and less water is lost, which fits the plants' need to save water.

title: The growth of public libraries
subject: Social history
text: In the nineteenth century, books were expensive, and most working people could not afford to buy many. Public libraries changed this by offering books free to anyone who lived in a town. Supporters argued that libraries would improve education and help people find better jobs. Some critics worried that libraries would mainly lend popular novels rather than serious works. In practice, they did both: novels were the most borrowed books, but libraries also gave many people their first access to books on science, history and technical trades.

questions.stem: What did critics worry about?
choices: Libraries would mainly lend popular novels
Libraries would cost too much
Libraries would close quickly
Libraries would only serve the rich
questions.explanation: Critics worried libraries would mainly lend popular novels rather than serious works.

questions.stem: What does the author suggest about the critics' worry?
choices: It was partly true but missed other benefits
It was completely correct
It was completely wrong
It caused libraries to close
questions.explanation: Novels were the most borrowed, but libraries also gave access to serious books, so the worry was partly true.

title: Animal migration
subject: Zoology
text: Every year, many animals travel long distances between the places where they feed and the places where they breed. Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, a round trip of more than seventy thousand kilometers. How animals find their way remains an active area of research. Studies suggest they use several cues at once, including the position of the sun, patterns of stars, the earth's magnetic field and familiar landmarks. Young animals of some species migrate alone on their first trip, which suggests that part of this ability is inborn.

questions.stem: Which cue is NOT mentioned as helping animals navigate?
choices: The sound of the ocean
The position of the sun
The earth's magnetic field
Familiar landmarks
questions.explanation: The sun, stars, magnetic field and landmarks are listed; sound is not.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention young animals that migrate alone?
choices: To suggest that some navigation ability is inborn
To show that young animals are strong
To explain why terns fly so far
To describe the dangers of migration
questions.explanation: Young animals finding their way alone suggests the ability is partly inborn.
